ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are two shapes composed of the same gray pieces. In the left shape, one can see a vertically placed rectangular region, as well as quarter-circle arcs extending outward; several straight edges are exposed on the outside, including vertical long edges and horizontal short edges. The right shape is like an arched-top shape, with the upper part composed of two larger quarter-circle arcs, smaller quarter-circle arcs on the lower parts of the two sides, and a segment of horizontal straight edge exposed on the outside at the bottom. Reasoning: The two figures are composed of the same 5 pieces: one 5 cm × 10 cm rectangle, two large quarter-circles with radius 10 cm, and two small quarter-circles with radius 5 cm. In both figures, the arcs of the four quarter-circles are all on the outer boundary, so the total length of the curved parts is the same, and they cancel each other out when finding the perimeter difference. Only compare the exposed straight edges: the exposed straight edges of the left figure are two long radius edges of 10 cm and two short radius edges of 5 cm, with total length 10+10+5+5=30 cm; the exposed straight edge of the right figure is only the rectangle's bottom edge 10 cm. Therefore the perimeter difference of the two figures is 30−10=20 cm.

raw_record.question_text: Both the figures on the right were made out of the same 5 pieces. The rectangle has dimensions $5 \mathrm{~cm} \times 10 \mathrm{~cm}$. The other pieces are quarter circles with 2 different sized radii. What is the difference between the perimeters of the two figures?

method.method_draft: Direct outer-boundary tracing. First read the diagram: each figure is built from the same central 5 cm by 10 cm rectangle, two large quarter-circles whose radii match the 10 cm side, and two small quarter-circles whose radii match the 5 cm side. In both figures, all four curved quarter-circle arcs appear on the outside boundary, so their total curved length is identical and cancels in the perimeter difference. Then compare only the exposed straight boundary segments. In the left figure, the exposed straight segments are two long radius edges of length 10 cm and two short radius edges of length 5 cm, totaling 30 cm. In the right figure, the only exposed straight segment is the bottom side of the rectangle, length 10 cm. The perimeter difference is therefore 30-10=20 cm.

method.method_draft: Shared-edge subtraction method. Read from the image that the five pieces are the 5 by 10 rectangle plus two quarter-circles of radius 10 and two quarter-circles of radius 5. Instead of tracing the outside, start with the total perimeter of all five separate pieces, which is the same for both figures. A joined edge disappears from the outside perimeter twice, once for each piece sharing it. In the left figure, the diagram shows the rectangle sharing its two long sides with the two large quarter-circles, for 10+10 cm, and its two short sides with the two small quarter-circles, for 5+5 cm, so the total shared length is 30 cm. In the right figure, the internal joins total 40 cm: the two large quarter-circles share a vertical radius of 10 cm, their lower straight radii together form a 20 cm seam across the lower row, and the rectangle shares two 5 cm sides with the small quarter-circles. Thus the right figure has 10 cm more shared edge than the left, so its outer perimeter is smaller by 2*10=20 cm. The difference is 20 cm.
